notes:
1. Population — Meaning and Development Significance

  • Population refers to the total number of people living in a specified geographical area at a particular point in time.
  • Population is both an economic resource and a development responsibility.
  • A large population can contribute to growth when people are healthy, educated, skilled and productively employed.
📌 Must-Memorise

Population → Human Resource + Development Responsibility

2. Demography — Meaning

  • Demography is the systematic study of population.
  • It examines population size, composition, distribution and change.

Important demographic characteristics include:

  • Age.
  • Sex.
  • Births.
  • Deaths.
  • Fertility.
  • Migration.
  • Literacy.
  • Occupation.
  • Rural–urban residence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Demography → Scientific Study of Population

3. Population Policy — Modern Approach

Modern population policy focuses on:

  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Reproductive choice.
  • Gender equality.
  • Employment.
  • Human development.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Population Policy ≠ Merely Reducing Population Numbers

4. Population and Development — Two-Way Relationship

  • Better education and health can change fertility and mortality patterns.
  • Demographic changes affect economic growth, employment, infrastructure and public expenditure.
  • Population and development therefore influence one another.

5. Census — Meaning

  • A Census is an official systematic enumeration of population and its demographic, social and economic characteristics.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census → Official Population Enumeration

6. Indian Census — Decennial Tradition

  • India has maintained a regular decennial Census tradition since 1881.
  • A Census is normally conducted once every ten years.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Census → Decennial

Regular Census Tradition → Since 1881

7. Census Act — 1948

  • Post-Independence Censuses are conducted under the Census Act, 1948.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census Act → 1948

8. Census Authority

  • The Census is conducted under the authority of the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India.
  • It functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census → Registrar General & Census Commissioner → Ministry of Home Affairs

9. Uses of Census Data

Census information supports:

  • Population planning.
  • Administration.
  • Welfare planning.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Health.
  • Education.
  • Housing.
  • Urban planning.
  • Research.

10. Census vs Projection vs Survey

  • Census → Actual official enumeration.
  • Population projection → Statistical estimate of future population.
  • Survey → Data collected from a sample.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Census ≠ Projection ≠ Sample Survey

11. Census 2011 — India Population

  • Census 2011 recorded India's population at 1,210,854,977, or approximately 121.09 crore.
  • It included about 623.27 million males and 587.58 million females.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Population — Census 2011 → ≈ 121.09 Crore

12. Census 2011 — Historical Position

  • Census 2011 was the 15th Census in India's continuous Census series.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census 2011 → 15th Census

13. Census 2011 — Data Rule

  • Census 2011 is a completed Census benchmark.
  • Census figures must always be identified by Census year.
  • Census 2011 population should not be described as India's present population.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Census 2011 Figure ≠ Current Population Estimate

14. Population Change — Basic Formula

Population change is determined by:

Births − Deaths + Net Migration

📌 Must-Memorise

Population Change = Births − Deaths + Net Migration

15. Natural Increase

  • Natural increase means the excess of births over deaths.
  • Migration is excluded.
📌 Must-Memorise

Natural Increase = Births − Deaths

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Natural Increase ≠ Total Population Change

16. Population Size vs Population Growth

  • Population size → Total number of people.
  • Population growth → Change in population over time.
  • A country can have a very large population but a relatively low growth rate.

17. Decadal Growth Rate

  • Decadal growth rate means percentage change in population over a ten-year period.
  • It is particularly important in Indian Census comparisons because the Census is normally decennial.

18. Population Explosion

  • Population explosion refers to exceptionally rapid population growth over a relatively short period.
  • In India, the term is historically associated with mortality falling significantly while fertility remained relatively high.

19. Why India's Population Grew Rapidly

Important causes included:

  • Declining mortality.
  • Better control of epidemics.
  • Vaccination.
  • Improved public health.
  • Better food availability.
  • Medical advances.
  • Fertility declining more slowly than mortality.

20. Population — Resource or Burden?

Population becomes a productive resource when supported by:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Skills.
  • Employment.

Population can create development pressure when growth exceeds provision of:

  • Jobs.
  • Housing.
  • Education.
  • Health care.
  • Food.
  • Water.
  • Infrastructure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Population Impact → Depends on Human Capital + Employment

21. Population Density — Meaning

  • Population density means the number of persons living per unit of geographical area.
  • In India, it is usually expressed as persons per square kilometre.
📌 Must-Memorise

Population Density = Population ÷ Land Area

22. India — Population Density in Census 2011

  • Census 2011 recorded India's density at approximately 382 persons per square kilometre.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Density — 2011 → 382 per sq km

23. Factors Affecting Population Distribution

Population distribution is influenced by:

  • Relief.
  • Climate.
  • Water.
  • Soil fertility.
  • Agricultural productivity.
  • Industrialisation.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Transport.
  • Employment opportunities.

24. Population Size vs Density

  • Population size → Total number of people.
  • Population density → Persons per unit area.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Largest Population ≠ Highest Density

25. Sex Ratio — Census Meaning

  • In Indian Census usage, sex ratio means the number of females per 1,000 males.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sex Ratio → Females per 1,000 Males

26. India — Sex Ratio in Census 2011

  • India's overall sex ratio in Census 2011 was 943 females per 1,000 males.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Sex Ratio — 2011 → 943

27. Child Sex Ratio

  • Child sex ratio generally means the number of girls per 1,000 boys in the 0–6 age group under Census terminology.
📌 Must-Memorise

Child Sex Ratio → Girls per 1,000 Boys, Age 0–6

28. Sex Ratio at Birth

  • Sex ratio at birth measures the sex composition of live births.
  • It is different from both overall Census sex ratio and child sex ratio.

29. Three Sex-Ratio Measures

  • Overall sex ratio → Females per 1,000 males in total population.
  • Child sex ratio → Girls per 1,000 boys aged 0–6.
  • Sex ratio at birth → Female live births relative to male live births.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Overall Sex Ratio ≠ Child Sex Ratio ≠ Sex Ratio at Birth

30. Literacy — Census Meaning

  • Literacy is an important demographic and human-development indicator.
  • Census literacy measurement concerns persons aged 7 years and above.
📌 Must-Memorise

Literacy Rate → Population Aged 7+

31. India — Literacy Rate in Census 2011

  • Census 2011 recorded India's literacy rate at approximately 74.04%.
📌 Must-Memorise

India Literacy — 2011 → 74.04%

32. Literacy vs Education

  • Literacy refers to basic ability to read and write with understanding under Census methodology.
  • Education is broader and includes schooling, higher education, skills and learning.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Literacy ≠ Educational Attainment

33. Female Education — Demographic Importance

Higher female education is often associated with:

  • Better health awareness.
  • Improved child nutrition.
  • Lower infant mortality.
  • Delayed marriage.
  • Lower fertility.
  • Greater use of health services.
  • Greater employment opportunities.

34. Age Composition

  • Age composition means distribution of population among age groups.
  • Population can broadly be divided into:
  • Children.
  • Working-age population.
  • Elderly population.

35. Why Age Structure Matters

A large child population requires more:

  • Education.
  • Nutrition.
  • Immunisation.
  • Child health services.

A large working-age population requires:

  • Skills.
  • Employment.

A growing elderly population requires:

  • Pensions.
  • Health care.
  • Long-term care.
  • Social support.

36. Dependency Ratio

  • Dependency ratio compares dependent-age population with working-age population.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dependency Ratio = Dependent-Age Population ÷ Working-Age Population

37. Child and Old-Age Dependency

Dependency can be divided into:

  • Child dependency.
  • Old-age dependency.
  • Demographic transition can initially reduce child dependency and later increase old-age dependency.

38. Crude Birth Rate — CBR

  • CBR stands for Crude Birth Rate.
  • It measures live births during a year per 1,000 population.
📌 Must-Memorise

CBR → Live Births per 1,000 Population

39. Crude Death Rate — CDR

  • CDR stands for Crude Death Rate.
  • It measures deaths during a year per 1,000 population.
📌 Must-Memorise

CDR → Deaths per 1,000 Population

40. Why Birth and Death Rates Are Called Crude

  • Crude rates are calculated for the overall population without fully adjusting for differences in age composition.
  • They should therefore be interpreted alongside age-specific indicators.

41. Fertility — Meaning

  • Fertility refers to actual childbearing in a population.

42. Total Fertility Rate — TFR

  • TFR stands for Total Fertility Rate.
  • It estimates the average number of children a woman would bear during her reproductive years if prevailing age-specific fertility rates continued.
📌 Must-Memorise

TFR → Average Children per Woman under Prevailing Fertility Rates

43. Replacement-Level Fertility

  • Replacement-level fertility is the fertility level at which a population broadly replaces itself from one generation to the next in the absence of migration.
  • Under relatively low mortality, it is commonly approximated at about 2.1 children per woman.
📌 Must-Memorise

Replacement-Level Fertility → ≈ 2.1

44. Population Momentum

  • Population can continue growing even after fertility reaches replacement level.
  • This occurs when a large number of young people enter reproductive ages.
📌 Must-Memorise

Population Momentum → Growth Continues After Fertility Falls

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Replacement Fertility ≠ Immediate Zero Population Growth

45. Mortality — Meaning

  • Mortality refers to deaths occurring in a population.
  • Declining mortality was an important factor behind India's earlier rapid population growth.

46. Infant Mortality Rate — IMR

  • IMR stands for Infant Mortality Rate.
  • It measures deaths of infants below one year per 1,000 live births.
📌 Must-Memorise

IMR → Infant Deaths Below Age 1 per 1,000 Live Births

47. What IMR Indicates

IMR reflects conditions relating to:

  • Maternal health.
  • Child health.
  • Nutrition.
  • Sanitation.
  • Health-system access.
  • Socio-economic development.

48. Maternal Mortality Ratio — MMR

  • Maternal Mortality Ratio is conventionally expressed as maternal deaths per 100,000 live births according to the prescribed statistical definition.
📌 Must-Memorise

MMR → Per 100,000 Live Births

49. IMR vs MMR

  • IMR → Infant deaths below one year per 1,000 live births.
  • MMR → Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

IMR Denominator Scale ≠ MMR Denominator Scale

50. Life Expectancy at Birth

  • Life expectancy at birth means the average number of years a newborn would be expected to live if prevailing mortality conditions continued.
  • Rising life expectancy generally reflects improved survival but also contributes to population ageing.

51. Demographic Transition — Meaning

  • Demographic Transition Theory explains the long-term movement from high birth and death rates towards low birth and death rates as societies develop.
📌 Must-Memorise

High Birth + High Death

→ Death Falls

→ Rapid Growth

→ Birth Falls

→ Slow Growth / Ageing

52. Demographic Transition — Early Stage

  • Birth rates are high.
  • Death rates are high.
  • Population growth remains relatively low.

53. Mortality-Decline Stage

  • Death rates fall because of better food, sanitation, public health and medicine.
  • Birth rates remain high.
  • Population therefore grows rapidly.

54. Fertility-Decline Stage

Birth rates fall because of factors such as:

  • Urbanisation.
  • Female education.
  • Lower infant mortality.
  • Contraception.
  • Changing family preferences.
  • Population growth begins to slow.

55. Low-Fertility Stage

  • Birth and death rates become relatively low.
  • Population growth becomes slow and may eventually become zero or negative.
  • Population ageing becomes increasingly important.

56. Indian States — Different Demographic Stages

  • Indian States do not necessarily pass through demographic transition at the same time.
  • Some States retain younger populations, while others face more rapid ageing.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

India's Demographic Transition ≠ Uniform Across All States

57. Demographic Dividend — Meaning

  • Demographic dividend is the potential economic benefit arising when the working-age share becomes relatively large compared with the dependent population.
📌 Must-Memorise

Demographic Dividend → Favourable Working-Age Structure

58. Demographic Dividend — Not Automatic

A demographic dividend requires:

  • Education.
  • Nutrition.
  • Health.
  • Skills.
  • Employment.
  • Women's participation.
  • Investment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Working-Age Population + Skills + Jobs + Health → Dividend

59. When Demographic Dividend Becomes Pressure

  • A large working-age population without sufficient skills and jobs can create unemployment and social pressure.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Large Youth Population ≠ Automatic Demographic Dividend

60. Human Capital

  • Human capital refers to people's education, skills, health, knowledge and productive capabilities.
  • Strong human capital is essential for converting population into economic strength.

61. Women's Participation and Demographic Dividend

  • Greater female education and employment can significantly strengthen demographic gains.
  • Structural barriers that keep working-age women outside productive employment can reduce the potential dividend.

62. Population Ageing — Meaning

  • Population ageing means an increase in the proportion of elderly persons in the population.

It generally results from:

  • Declining fertility.
  • Increasing life expectancy.
  • Large generations moving into older age groups.

63. Population Ageing — Policy Needs

Ageing increases demand for:

  • Geriatric health care.
  • Pensions.
  • Social assistance.
  • Long-term care.
  • Accessible housing.
  • Elder-friendly transport.
  • Community support.

64. Demographic Dividend to Ageing

The long-term transition can be understood as:

Large Child Population

→ Large Working-Age Population

→ Larger Elderly Population

📌 Must-Memorise

Demographic Dividend → Temporary Window, Not Permanent Condition

65. Urbanisation — Meaning

  • Urbanisation means an increase in the proportion of population living in urban areas.

It can occur through:

  • Natural growth of urban populations.
  • Rural-to-urban migration.
  • Expansion of urban boundaries.
  • Reclassification of settlements.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Urbanisation ≠ Rural-to-Urban Migration Alone

66. Census Towns

  • Some settlements can acquire urban status for Census purposes when they satisfy prescribed demographic and occupational criteria even without being statutory municipalities.
  • Urbanisation can therefore rise partly through reclassification.

67. Urbanisation — Benefits and Pressures

Urban areas can provide:

  • Employment.
  • Education.
  • Health care.
  • Markets.
  • Transport.
  • Technology.

Rapid urban growth can create pressure on:

  • Housing.
  • Water.
  • Sanitation.
  • Transport.
  • Waste management.
  • Air quality.
  • Infrastructure.

68. Migration — Meaning and Types

Migration can be:

  • Rural–rural.
  • Rural–urban.
  • Urban–urban.
  • Urban–rural.
  • Intra-State.
  • Inter-State.
  • International.

69. Push and Pull Factors

Push factors include:

  • Unemployment.
  • Low income.
  • Agricultural distress.
  • Natural disasters.
  • Conflict.
  • Poor services.

Pull factors include:

  • Employment.
  • Higher wages.
  • Education.
  • Better services.
  • Urban opportunities.

70. Migration — Economic Effects

Migration can:

  • Improve labour allocation.
  • Move workers towards higher-productivity opportunities.
  • Generate remittances.

Migrants can also face:

  • Informal employment.
  • Poor housing.
  • Weak social protection.
  • Language barriers.
  • Difficulty accessing services.

71. National Population Policy — 2000

  • India adopted the National Population Policy in 2000.
  • The supplied source describes it as emphasising reproductive health, voluntary and informed choice and a holistic, target-free approach to family planning.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Population Policy → 2000

72. National Population Policy — Broad Approach

Important areas include:

  • Reproductive health.
  • Contraceptive choice.
  • Maternal health.
  • Child health.
  • Education.
  • Delayed marriage.
  • Reduction of infant and maternal mortality.
  • Birth and death registration.
  • Population stabilisation.

73. Population Stabilisation

  • Population stabilisation means movement towards a sustainable and relatively stable demographic condition.
  • It does not require coercive restrictions on family size.
📌 Must-Memorise

Population Stabilisation → Voluntary + Human-Development Approach

74. Fertility Decline — Long-Term Drivers

Long-term fertility decline is closely connected with:

Women's Education

  • Child Survival
  • Health Services
  • Reproductive Choice
  • Economic Development

  • Tamil Nadu's Census 2011 population was 72,147,030, or approximately 7.21 crore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Population — 2011 → ≈ 7.21 Crore

76. Tamil Nadu — Population Density

  • Tamil Nadu's population density in Census 2011 was 555 persons per square kilometre.
  • This was above India's 2011 density of 382.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Density — 2011 → 555 per sq km

77. Tamil Nadu — Sex Ratio

  • Tamil Nadu's overall sex ratio in Census 2011 was 996 females per 1,000 males.
  • India's corresponding figure was 943.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Sex Ratio — 2011 → 996

78. Tamil Nadu — Urbanisation

  • Approximately 48.40% of Tamil Nadu's population was classified as urban in Census 2011.
  • About 51.60% was rural.
  • Tamil Nadu was therefore already highly urbanised by 2011.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Urban Share — 2011 → ≈ 48.40%

79. Tamil Nadu — Decadal Population Growth

  • Tamil Nadu's population increased by approximately 15.61% between Census 2001 and Census 2011 according to the supplied source.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Decadal Growth, 2001–11 → ≈ 15.61%

80. Tamil Nadu — Advanced Demographic Transition

  • Tamil Nadu has moved further through demographic transition than many parts of India.
  • Its demographic pattern is increasingly characterised by:
  • Lower fertility.
  • Slower population growth.
  • High urbanisation.
  • Increasing population ageing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu → Lower Fertility → Slower Growth → Ageing

81. Tamil Nadu — Ageing Challenge

  • According to projections referenced in the supplied source, Tamil Nadu is expected to have a relatively high elderly share by 2036.

This increases the importance of:

  • Elderly health care.
  • Social security.
  • Long-term care.
  • Accessible infrastructure.
  • Productive employment for the current working-age population.

82. Census 2027 — Current Source-Dated Status

According to the supplied source:

  • India's next Census is being conducted as Census of India 2027.
  • The Houselisting and Housing Census phase is scheduled during 1 April 2026 to 30 September 2026 across notified areas.
  • The exercise includes digital enumeration arrangements and self-enumeration facilities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Census 2027 → Ongoing Exercise in Supplied 2026 Source

83. Census 2027 — Important Data Rule

  • Until final Census 2027 demographic results are officially released, they should not be invented or replaced with projections.
  • Census 2011 remains a completed Census benchmark in the supplied material.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Census 2027 Exercise ≠ Final Census 2027 Population Results

85. Population Challenges — Employment and Skills

  • A large working-age population requires adequate productive jobs.
  • A large youth population also creates demand for:
  • Schools.
  • Colleges.
  • Vocational training.
  • Skills.
  • Education quality matters as much as enrolment.

86. Population Challenges — Health and Ageing

Population growth increases demand for:

  • Health infrastructure.
  • Maternal and child health services.

Population ageing shifts demand towards:

  • Chronic-disease care.
  • Geriatric care.
  • Long-term support.
  • Pensions.

87. Population Challenges — Urban Infrastructure

Urban population growth requires:

  • Housing.
  • Public transport.
  • Drinking water.
  • Sewerage.
  • Waste management.
  • Health facilities.
  • Other urban infrastructure.

88. Regional Demographic Differences

  • Younger States may require greater investment in schooling, maternal health, skills and jobs.
  • More advanced-transition States such as Tamil Nadu increasingly need elderly welfare and labour-force sustainability.

89. Gender and Population Development

Population outcomes are closely connected with:

  • Female education.
  • Employment.
  • Reproductive autonomy.
  • Maternal health.
  • Safety.
  • Gender equality.

90. Population and Environment

Population and consumption can create pressure on:

  • Water.
  • Land.
  • Energy.
  • Housing.
  • Waste systems.
  • Natural ecosystems.

However, environmental pressure also depends on:

  • Consumption patterns.
  • Technology.
  • Resource efficiency.

100. TNPSC Traps

  • Population and population density are different.
  • Population size and population growth rate are different.
  • Natural increase excludes migration.
  • Census, projection and survey are different.
  • Census 2011 figures should be labelled as Census 2011.
  • India's Census is normally decennial.
  • Census Act → 1948.
  • Census 2011 → 15th Census.
  • India population in Census 2011 → ≈121.09 crore.
  • India density in Census 2011 → 382 per sq km.
  • India's overall sex ratio in Census 2011 → 943.
  • India's literacy rate in Census 2011 → 74.04%.
  • Overall sex ratio and child sex ratio are different.
  • Sex ratio at birth is another separate indicator.
  • Census sex ratio → Females per 1,000 males.
  • Child sex ratio → Girls per 1,000 boys aged 0–6.
  • Literacy and educational attainment are different.
  • CBR and TFR are not the same.
  • TFR does not mean every woman actually has that number of children.
  • Replacement fertility does not mean zero fertility.
  • Replacement fertility does not immediately stop population growth.
  • Population momentum explains continued growth after fertility decline.
  • IMR is per 1,000 live births.
  • MMR is per 100,000 live births.
  • Demographic dividend does not mean merely having a large population.
  • Demographic dividend requires skills, health and jobs.
  • Population ageing results from both lower fertility and longer life expectancy.
  • Urbanisation is not identical to rural-to-urban migration.
  • Migration includes several internal and international forms.
  • National Population Policy → 2000.
  • Modern family planning emphasises informed and voluntary choice.

  • Is demographic dividend automatic? → No.

  • Urbanisation means? → Increase in proportion living in urban areas.
  • Can urbanisation occur without migration? → Yes, through natural growth, boundary expansion and reclassification.
  • Migration types? → Rural-rural, rural-urban, urban-urban, urban-rural, intra-State, inter-State and international.
  • Push factors? → Unemployment, distress, disasters and poor services.
  • Pull factors? → Jobs, higher wages, education and better services.
